title: Effect of Carbohydrate Intake on Half-Marathon Performance of Well-Trained Runners
authors: Burke LM, Wood C, Pyne DB, Telford RD, Saunders PU
journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
population: 18 highly trained runners who ran two half marathons 3 weeks apart in mild conditions (about 74 min to finish, from 40 s being 0.9%)
findings: Each runner ran two half marathons, taking either a flavoured placebo drink (about 426 mL) or water (about 386 mL) plus a commercial gel supplying 1.1 +/- 0.2 g/kg body mass of carbohydrate.
Compared with placebo the gel improved time by 0.3% or 14 s, which was not significant (P = 0.52).
Three runners complained of gastrointestinal discomfort in the gel trial, which produced a clear impairment of performance by 2.4% or 105 s (P = 0.03).
The authors say benefits to half-marathon performance were not detected and that the theoretical improvement during 1 h exercise with carbohydrate merits further investigation.
limitations: Fast, highly trained runners (about 74 min), well under the 90 to 120 min of most recreational half marathons; 18 subjects; the second race was 0.9% faster whatever the drink (a learning order effect); one gel dose given as a single total.
implications: The one half-marathon carbohydrate trial in the corpus found no significant gain from about 1.1 g/kg of gel in a roughly 74-minute race, and a loss in the three runners who had stomach trouble. It supports leaving a rate off for a half marathon in this band; it does not test a 90 to 120 minute finisher.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (IJSNEM 15:573-589). Abstract read on Europe PMC. The finish time is not stated in the abstract; 'about 74 min' is computed from 40 s equal to 0.9% and is flagged as derived. Crossref lists no correction, erratum or retraction notice (checked 2026-11-16).
